text: In the very early days, people will discount till the cows come home because they think that's the way to get a deal done. The best clients are not going to do that to you.
speaker: Jen Abel
context: Lenny mentions that most founders would rather get 10 ten-thousand-dollar deals than lose nine and get one hundred-thousand-dollar deal. Jen explains why this approach is problematic for enterprise sales. She argues that discounting heavily signals weakness and attracts the wrong type of clients who aren't truly committed to the product's value.
text_ko: 초창기엔 거래를 따내려고 사람들이 계속 가격을 깎아요. 하지만 최고의 고객들은 그렇게 하진 않아요.
text_zh: 在刚起步的时候，很多人会不停地压价，因为他们以为只有这样才能谈成生意。真正优质的客户不会这么对你。
text_es: Al principio, mucha gente te pedirá descuentos hasta el cansancio porque creen que así se cierra el trato. Los mejores clientes no te van a hacer eso.
key_sentence: The best clients are not going to do that to you.
original_text: In the very early days, people will discount till the cows come home because they think that's the way to get a deal done. The best clients are not going to do that to you. If they're sitting there nickel-and-diming you, they're not fully bought in on what you're selling them.

vocabulary.definition: A reduction in the usual price of a product or service, often used as an incentive to encourage purchases.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, discounts are frequently employed as a marketing strategy to increase sales volume or attract new customers, particularly in competitive markets.
vocabulary.nuance: While offering discounts can boost short-term sales, excessive discounting may devalue a brand or product in the eyes of consumers.

vocabulary.definition: To successfully complete a transaction or agreement, often involving negotiation and compromise.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business negotiations, getting a deal done is crucial for establishing partnerships, closing sales, or finalizing contracts, highlighting the importance of effective communication and persuasion.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase implies a sense of urgency and the necessity of overcoming obstacles to achieve a mutually beneficial outcome.

text: As soon as you become a comparison, as soon as you become one of three that they're testing out, you've already sort of lost. It's all about differentiation.
speaker: Jen Abel
context: Jen is explaining how to position your product in enterprise sales. She emphasizes that once a potential client starts comparing your solution to others in a competitive evaluation process, you've lost your advantage. The key is to differentiate yourself by focusing on future opportunities and outcomes rather than competing on features or price.
text_ko: 사람들이 비교 대상으로 삼아 세 가지 옵션 중 하나로 시험해보는 순간, 이미 진 거나 다름없어요. 핵심은 차별화(differentiation)이에요.
text_zh: 一旦你被拿来做比较，或者只是他们在试的三选一，你基本就输了。关键是要有差异化(differentiation)。
text_es: En cuanto te ponen como una más para comparar, en cuanto eres uno de los tres que están probando, ya has perdido terreno. Todo es cuestión de diferenciación (differentiation).
key_sentence: You've sort of lost when becoming one of three testing out.
original_text: As soon as you become a comparison, as soon as you become one of three that they're testing out, you've already sort of lost. It's all about differentiation. Here's what you will be able to do tomorrow because of how we're going to serve you today.

vocabulary.definition: The process of distinguishing a product or service from others to make it more attractive to a specific target market.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, differentiation is crucial for establishing a unique value proposition that sets a company apart from its competitors, particularly in saturated markets.
vocabulary.nuance: While differentiation often refers to tangible features, it can also encompass branding and customer experience; avoid using it in contexts where competition is not a factor.

text: Enterprise is the number one thing they buy services, they know how to do it's super easy, they do it all of the time. It's like the most consistent thing they do. It's their largest budget item, external resources, consultants, whatever.
speaker: Jen Abel
context: Lenny asks about Jen's advice to start with services rather than just selling software products to enterprises. Jen explains that large companies are very comfortable buying services and consulting - it's something they do regularly and have large budgets for. This makes services an easier entry point than trying to sell new technology solutions.
text_ko: 기업(enterprise)은 서비스 구매가 가장 큰 비중이에요. 어떻게 하는지 잘 알고 있어서 아주 손쉽게 처리해요. 늘 하던 일이니까요. 가장 일관되게 하는 활동이고, 예산도 가장 큰 항목이에요. 외부 리소스(external resources)나 컨설턴트(consultants) 같은 데에 많이 쓰여요.
text_zh: 大企业买服务这事儿是他们的强项，轻车熟路的，天天都在做。这是他们最稳定的操作了，也是预算里最大的一块 - 外部资源啊、咨询啊什么的。
text_es: Las empresas grandes son las que más compran servicios, ya saben cómo hacerlo y es súper fácil para ellas, lo hacen todo el tiempo. Es como lo más constante que hacen. Es su partida presupuestaria más grande: recursos externos, consultores, lo que sea.
key_sentence: Enterprise is their largest budget item for external resources.

vocabulary.definition: Assets or services sourced from outside an organization, rather than being produced internally.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, external resources can include freelancers, consultants, or outsourced services that help companies achieve their goals without the need for permanent staff.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a reliance on outside expertise or support, which can be seen as both a strength and a potential risk if not managed properly.

vocabulary.definition: Professionals who provide expert advice in a particular area, often hired on a temporary basis to assist organizations.
vocabulary.businessContext: Consultants are commonly used in business settings to offer specialized knowledge, help with strategic planning, or improve operational efficiency.
vocabulary.nuance: While consultants can bring valuable insights, their effectiveness can vary based on their understanding of the client's specific context and needs.

vocabulary.definition: A specific line item in a financial plan that allocates funds for a particular expense or category.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, budget items help organizations track spending and ensure that resources are allocated effectively to meet strategic objectives.
vocabulary.nuance: The term suggests a level of detail in financial planning, indicating that each item is scrutinized for its necessity and impact on overall financial health.

vocabulary.definition: Showing steady conformity to the same principles, course, or form; reliable and predictable in performance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, consistency is crucial for maintaining quality, building brand trust, and ensuring customer satisfaction over time.
vocabulary.nuance: While consistency is generally viewed positively, it can also imply a lack of innovation or adaptability if taken to an extreme.

text: It's more of an art. It's all about deal crafting. It is a relationship you're building with someone. If they know they can call on you, people will turn over rocks for you.
speaker: Jen Abel
context: Lenny mentions that Jen talks about enterprise sales being very creative. Jen responds by explaining that enterprise sales is more of an art than a science, requiring creativity in structuring deals and building deep relationships. She shares a real example of how a strong relationship with a Fortune 10 client led them to expedite a deal specifically to help her, demonstrating the power of relationship-based selling.
text_ko: 이건 기술이라기보다 감각적인 일이에요. 결국 딜 설계(deal crafting)이 핵심이에요. 사람과의 관계를 쌓아가는 과정이에요. 믿고 도움을 청할 수 있다는 걸 알면 사람들은 당신을 위해 발 벗고 나서줘요.
text_zh: 这更像门艺术，关键在于怎么把交易做成 (deal crafting)。本质上是在跟人建立关系。如果别人知道可以随时找你帮忙，他们就会为你千方百计、到处跑资源。
text_es: Es más un arte. Todo es cuestión de cómo se diseñan los acuerdos (deal crafting). Es una relación que estás construyendo con alguien. Si saben que pueden contar contigo, la gente moverá cielo y tierra por ti.
key_sentence: It's all about deal crafting and building relationships.
original_text: It's more of an art. It's all about deal crafting. It is a relationship you're building with someone. If they know they can call on you, people will turn over rocks for you. I have a client at a Fortune 10 company where I was like, 'It's so important we get the deal done this year. Is that possible?' And she's like, 'It's a tall order, but if it's going to help you, let's do it.' These are how enterprise deals gets done. It's relationships.

vocabulary.definition: The process of designing and negotiating a business agreement or transaction to meet the needs of all parties involved.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, deal crafting is crucial for creating win-win scenarios that foster long-term partnerships and successful outcomes in negotiations.
vocabulary.nuance: This term implies a level of artistry and skill in negotiation, suggesting that successful deals require more than just basic transactional skills.

text: I want to email someone not in the database that's getting hit by a million folks. I want to take a back door in, not the front door where everyone else is trick or treating.
speaker: Jen Abel
context: Lenny asks about the state of the art in go-to-market outbound tooling. Jen explains why she doesn't use automated tools for prospecting. She believes that AI tools and databases are creating too much noise because they all target the same people. Instead, she prefers finding unique ways to reach prospects that others aren't using.
text_ko: 데이터베이스(database)가 이미 수많은 사람들에게 시달리고 있어서, 그 안에 없는 사람에게 이메일을 보내고 싶어요. 다들 우르르 몰려가는 앞문(front door)으로 가지 않고 백도어(back door)로 슬쩍 들어가고 싶어요.
text_zh: 我想给数据库里没有的人发邮件，不想走那些被无数人轰炸的渠道。我要走后门，不走正门——正门那儿人太多了，跟要糖的小孩似的排着队呢。
text_es: Quiero contactar por email a alguien que no está en la base de datos pero que está siendo bombardeado por un millón de personas. Quiero entrar por la puerta de atrás, no por la puerta principal donde todos están pidiendo dulces.
key_sentence: I want to take a back door in, not the front door.

text: The market doesn't want to be sold to, they want to buy. And I know that it's very hard to hire a really good enterprise salesperson.
speaker: Jen Abel
context: Jen is discussing what makes a good enterprise salesperson and why it's challenging to find the right people. She explains that taking typical salespeople and putting them in startup sales roles often fails because it feels too 'salesy' to prospects. She emphasizes that great enterprise salespeople are as rare as great founders or engineers.
text_ko: 시장은 판매당하는 걸 좋아하지 않고 스스로 사길 원해요. 그리고 정말 뛰어난 엔터프라이즈 영업 담당자(enterprise salesperson)를 채용하기가 얼마나 어려운지 잘 알아요.
text_zh: 客户不想被人推销，他们更想主动来买。我知道，要招到一个真正优秀的企业销售（enterprise salesperson）非常难。
text_es: Los clientes no quieren que les vendan; quieren comprar. Y sé que es muy difícil contratar a un buen comercial para cuentas empresariales (enterprise salesperson).
key_sentence: The market doesn't want to be sold to, they want to buy.
original_text: The market doesn't want to be sold to, they want to buy. And I know that it's very hard to hire a really good enterprise salesperson. The number of people that I've interviewed, I can count on my hand the ones that I get really, really excited by.

vocabulary.definition: An enterprise refers to a business or company, particularly one that is large and complex in nature. It often implies a level of organization and structure that is necessary for managing various operations and resources.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, 'enterprise' is frequently used to describe large-scale organizations that operate across multiple sectors or regions, often requiring sophisticated management and operational strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'enterprise' can also connote a sense of innovation and initiative, particularly in entrepreneurial contexts, distinguishing it from smaller businesses or startups.

vocabulary.definition: A salesperson is an individual whose primary responsibility is to sell products or services to customers, often through direct interaction and relationship-building.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business and sales, a salesperson plays a crucial role in driving revenue and fostering customer loyalty, often requiring skills in negotiation, communication, and product knowledge.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'salesperson' is a neutral term, it can sometimes carry a negative connotation if associated with aggressive or pushy sales tactics; thus, it is important to emphasize consultative selling approaches.
